Testing Middleware Without an App

validate.js is just a function that reads req and calls next() or res — a fake req/res object is enough.

validate.js (Figure 3.5) never touches Express internals directly — it reads req[part], and calls either next() or next(someError). That means testing it doesn't need supertest, or a running app, or even a real route: a plain object standing in for req, and a jest.fn() standing in for next, is a complete enough fake to call the middleware directly.

// Figure 3.16: calling middleware directly, with fakes for req/next (tests/unit/validate.middleware.test.js, excerpt)
const schema = z.object({ name: z.string().min(1) });

it('forwards a 400 ApiError with per-field details when the schema fails', () => {
  const req = { body: { name: '' }, params: {}, query: {} };
  const next = jest.fn();

  validate({ body: schema })(req, {}, next);

  const err = next.mock.calls[0][0];
  expect(err).toBeInstanceOf(ApiError);
  expect(err.status).toBe(400);
});

validate({ body: schema }) still returns the actual inner middleware function (Figure 3.5's (a) => (b) => ... shape) — calling it here as (req, {}, next) runs it exactly the way Express would, just with req built by hand instead of arriving over HTTP, and res passed as an empty object since this particular path through validate never touches it. next.mock.calls[0][0] reaches into Jest's own record of every call made to the next mock — [0] for the first call, [0] again for that call's first argument — to get at the actual error object validate passed through, and assert it's a real ApiError with the right status.

This test also deliberately uses a throwaway schema — z.object({ name: z.string().min(1) }) — instead of one of the real validators. The point here is what validate.js itself does with any schema's result, not any one resource's specific rules, which the previous slide's tests already cover on their own.
